How the calculators work

Each calculator starts from a common way of building the project, such as a deck with a ledger, joists in hangers and a dropped beam on 6x6 posts. From your sizes it works out every part with its nominal size, cut length and quantity. A cut list shows what to cut, a shopping list shows how many boards of which stock length to buy, with the offcuts used where they fit.

Lumber is listed by nominal size, the way it is sold: a 2x6 is actually 1-1/2 × 5-1/2 in. The drawings and the 3D view use the real dimensions.

Where the prices come from

The example prices are per linear foot at big-box home centers in November 2026, for pressure-treated pine, cedar, composite decking, whitewood and Douglas fir. Lumber prices change weekly and differ a lot between regions and between home centers and lumberyards. Use the price level field to scale all prices, for example to 120 % on the West Coast or after you have a quote from your yard.

What the sizes are based on

Deck joists and beams follow IRC Tables R507.6 and R507.5 for 40 psf live load. Patio covers and carports use the same tables, which is on the safe side for roofs in areas without heavy snow. The results are planning values to price and buy the job. Your building department has the final word, and in snow country or for anything unusual, an engineer.

Lumber sizes follow the span tables of the 2021 International Residential Code (IRC) and are planning values. They do not replace a permit review or an engineer. Decks, patio covers and carports usually need a building permit, so check with your local building department.
